title: Κορώνη καὶ κόραξ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 170. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κορώνη φθονήσασα κόρακι ἐπὶ τῷ διὰ οἰωνῶν μαντεύεσθαι ἀνθρώποις καὶ τὸ μέλλον προφαίνειν καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ὑπ’ αὐτῶν μαρτυρεῖσθαι, ἐβουλήθη τῶν αὐτῶν ἐφικέσθαι· καὶ δὴ θεασαμένη τινὰς ὁδοιπόρους παριόντας ἧκεν ἐπί τινος δένδρου, καὶ στᾶσα μεγάλα ἐκεκράγει.
sentences.tr: Korōnē phthonēsasa koraki epi tōi dia oiōnōn manteuesthai anthrōpois kai to mellon prophainein kai dia touto hyp’ autōn martyreisthai, eboulēthē tōn autōn ephikesthai· kai dē theasamenē tinas hodoiporous pariontas hēken epi tinos dendrou, kai stasa megala ekekragei.
sentences.l: A crow, having envied a raven for his divining by omens for men and revealing what is to come and being on that account well spoken of by them, wished to attain the same things; and so, having seen some travellers passing by, she came onto a tree, and taking her stand was shrieking loudly.
sentences.i: A crow envied the raven, because he divined by omens for men and disclosed what was to come, and was well thought of by them for it; and she wanted to attain as much herself. So, seeing some travellers going past, she settled on a tree, took her stand there, and set up a loud shrieking.
sentences.n: φθονέω takes the dative of the person envied (κόρακι) and ἐπί with the dative for what is envied. That second phrase is a single articular infinitive — the article τῷ turns the whole of μαντεύεσθαι … προφαίνειν … μαρτυρεῖσθαι into one noun for the preposition to govern. The fable takes for granted that the raven's cry counts as a bird-omen and the crow's does not; ancient bird-lore is in fact less tidy than that, and both birds appear in the omen lists, but the story needs the distinction and the traveller states it flatly. ἐκεκράγει is a pluperfect of κράζω carrying imperfect force: the perfect κέκραγα of this verb simply means "I am screeching". μεγάλα is a neuter plural doing adverbial duty, "loudly".

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ πρὸς τὴν φωνὴν ἐπιστραφέντων καὶ καταπλαγέντων, εἷς τις ὑποτυχὼν ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἀπίωμεν, ὦ φίλοι· κορώνη γάρ ἐστιν, ἥτις κεκραγυῖα οἰωνὸν οὐκ ἔχει. »
sentences.tr: Tōn de pros tēn phōnēn epistraphentōn kai kataplagentōn, heis tis hypotychōn ephē· « All’ apiōmen, ō philoi· korōnē gar estin, hētis kekraguia oiōnon ouk echei. »
sentences.l: And they having turned round towards the voice and been struck with alarm, one of them, taking-up-the-word, said: « Come, let us be off, friends; for it is a crow, which, though she screams, has no omen in her. »
sentences.i: And when they had turned toward the sound and taken fright, one of them spoke up: « Come, friends, let us be off — it is only a crow, and shriek as she may, there is no omen in her. »
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute, Τῶν δὲ … ἐπιστραφέντων καὶ καταπλαγέντων, both participles aorist passive. ἀπίωμεν is a hortatory subjunctive, "let us go", and the ἀλλά in front of it is the ordinary Greek nudge into action rather than a contrast — "come now". οἰωνὸν οὐκ ἔχει says the bird has no omen in her: her cry carries no meaning to read. κεκραγυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of the same κράζω as above, concessive here.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ τοῖς κρείττοσιν ἀνθαμιλλώμενοι πρὸς τῷ τῶν ἴσων μὴ ἐφικέσθαι, καὶ γέλωτα ὀφλισκάνουσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn hoi tois kreittosin anthamillōmenoi pros tōi tōn isōn mē ephikesthai, kai gelōta ophliskanousin.
sentences.l: So too those among men who contend against their betters, besides not attaining equality, also incur ridicule.
sentences.n: πρὸς τῷ … μὴ ἐφικέσθαι is another articular infinitive, negated by μή as infinitives are, and πρός with the dative here means "in addition to". ὀφλισκάνω γέλωτα is a fixed idiom, "to incur laughter", the verb belonging to the lawcourts, where one incurs a penalty — so the ridicule arrives like a sentence handed down. κρείττοσιν, "the stronger", is the ordinary Greek word for one's social betters.
